summary:
Coahuila de Zaragoza stands under the national framework of Mexico, where Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that most states now operate administrative procedures for legal gender recognition while warning that implementation differs sharply from one state to another. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2009.

Coahuila is one of the states that has legislated. The 2018 Law on the Civil Registry of the State of Coahuila, articles 124 to 128, established an administrative procedure for recognition of self-identified gender identity. The Human Rights Watch state-by-state tracker of March 2025 records it among the 32 states with such a procedure and links the official gazette text of the reform.

The procedure has been used at scale rather than existing on paper only. Coahuila's Civil Registry director, Ricardo Malacara, said on 31 March 2023 that roughly 1,500 people had completed the legal gender-identity change before the Civil Registry between early 2019 and March 2023, in both directions, male to female and female to male.

Document status does not resolve violence risk. More than 95% of homicides nationally went unpunished in 2022, and Transgender Europe's monitoring records 52 transfeminicidios in Mexico between October 2022 and September 2023, a figure second only to Brazil's 100. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and state authorities in 2024 to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded that LGBTI violations be investigated using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels.
tangentialFactors:
Human Rights Watch's report "I Just Want to Contribute to Society" (6 March 2024) provides the counter-case to Coahuila: in Tabasco no administrative procedure exists, the August 2023 killing of activist Karina Gómez remained unsolved, Tabasco's criminal code carries no hate-motivation provisions, and healthcare staff out patients by calling them by their legal names.

One neighbouring legislature has moved against the impunity figure. Mexico City made transfemicide a crime on 18 July 2024 with sentences of up to 70 years under the Paola Buenrostro law, named for a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished; the Guardian reported the statute on 24 July 2024 against a national backdrop in which more than 95% of homicides went unsolved in 2022.

Caroline Beer's analysis for LSE USAPP (22 November 2024) concludes that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice, and cautions that this must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.
localsOnly:
The 2018 reform was assembled in the Congress of Coahuila from proposals by several parliamentary groups together with an initiative by former governor Rubén Moreira. El Heraldo de Saltillo reported on 13 November 2018 that the dictamen was approved by unanimity, that it reforms article 133 of the Ley para la Familia de Coahuila de Zaragoza and creates the Ley del Registro Civil, and that article 2, fraction XI of the new law defines gender identity as the personal and internal conviction.

The same newspaper reported on 31 March 2023 that approximately 3,500 transgender citizens held formal jobs at companies operating in the state, alongside the roughly 1,500 completed registry changes recorded by the Civil Registry director from early 2019 to March 2023.

Human Rights Watch's March 2025 tracker situates the Coahuila statute alongside the Supreme Court rulings that drove the expansion of legal gender recognition across Mexico's states.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory addresses whether the Coahuila procedure has been refused, delayed or challenged in individual cases, nor whether any time limit, residency requirement or medical evidence applies to an application; the operating conditions of articles 124 to 128 are unresolved here.

Whether Coahuila's criminal code carries hate-motivation provisions, and whether the state has adopted any transfemicide offence comparable to Mexico City's July 2024 statute, is not sourced. The inventory contains no Coahuila-specific record of killings, assaults or police conduct toward trans people.

Access to gender-affirming healthcare, facility and bathroom rules, and the treatment of sex markers on federal documents such as passports are not covered by any source listed here. Usage figures stop at March 2023, so the current caseload of the Civil Registry procedure is unresolved.
